title: Model Monitoring and Drift Detection
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Model Monitoring and Drift Detection ##### Seven weeks of silent degradation A credit-risk model at an NBFC in Chennai fell from 0.41 PR-AUC to 0.19 over seven weeks. Nobody noticed. Every dashboard was green. The API returned 200s at 38 ms p95. Error rate was 0.02%. The model was serving predictions flawlessly — they were just increasingly wrong. The cause was upstream. A partner bureau changed how it reported `months_since_last_enquiry`: previously null when there had been no enquiry, now `-1`. The feature pipeline cast it to numeric, so `-1` sailed through as a valid value. The model read it as "enquired one month in the future" and inverted its risk ordering for that segment. Loan defaults take 90 days to materialise, so the label feedback that would have caught it was still eleven weeks away. By then ₹3.4 crore had been disbursed on inverted scores. **Software monitoring asks "is the service up?" Model monitoring asks "is the service still right?"** They are different questions, and the second one is harder because the answer usually arrives late. ##### Why models degrade Four mechanisms, and knowing which one you have determines the fix. **The world changes.** Customer behaviour shifts, competitors launch, regulations change, a pandemic happens. The relationship the model learned no longer holds. **The data pipeline changes.** A schema change, a unit change, a new sentinel value, a vendor switching format. The Chennai case. This is the most common cause and the most fixable. **Feedback loops.** The model's decisions reshape the data it will next be trained on. A fraud model that blocks certain transactions never observes their outcomes, so the next training set is biased by the current model's behaviour. **Adversarial adaptation.** Fraudsters, spammers and gaming users actively probe and adapt. Degradation here is not drift; it is an opponent. | Cause | Detectable by | Typical timescale | |---|---|---| | Pipeline change | Data quality checks | Immediate | | Data drift | Distribution monitoring | Days to weeks | | Concept drift | Performance monitoring, proxy labels | Weeks to months | | Feedback loop | Score distribution, business metrics | Months | | Adversarial | Sudden metric shifts, anomaly rate | Days | ##### The four monitoring layers ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Layer 1: SERVICE
uptime, latency, errors] -->|seconds| E[Alerting] B[Layer 2: DATA QUALITY
schema, ranges, nulls, volume] -->|minutes| E C[Layer 3: DRIFT
input + prediction distributions] -->|hours to days| E D[Layer 4: PERFORMANCE
metrics against actual labels] -->|days to months| E E --> F{Diagnose the cause} F -->|Pipeline broken| G[Fix upstream — do NOT retrain] F -->|Genuine concept drift| H[Retrain candidate] F -->|Neither| I[Investigate and document] ``` The organising insight: **signal speed is inverse to signal quality.** Service metrics arrive instantly and say nothing about correctness. Performance metrics are ground truth and arrive far too late. Layers 2 and 3 exist to bridge that gap — and the Chennai bug was a **layer 2** failure, catchable in hours. ##### Layer 2: data quality The fastest, cheapest and most effective layer, and the one most often skipped. ```python import pandera.pandas as pa from pandera.typing import Series import pandas as pd, numpy as np from prometheus_client import Gauge class ServingSchema(pa.DataFrameModel): monthly_income_inr: Series[float] = pa.Field(ge=1_000, le=10_000_000, nullable=True) # The Chennai contract, stated explicitly months_since_enquiry: Series[float] = pa.Field(ge=0, le=240, nullable=True) age: Series[int] = pa.Field(ge=18, le=100) credit_utilisation: Series[float] = pa.Field(ge=0, le=2.0) city_tier: Series[str] = pa.Field(isin=["1", "2", "3", "unknown"]) class Config: strict = "filter" coerce = True VIOLATIONS = Gauge("data_quality_violations", "", ["column", "check"]) NULL_RATE = Gauge("feature_null_rate", "", ["column"]) ROW_COUNT = Gauge("batch_row_count", "", ["source"]) def quality_check(df: pd.DataFrame, window: str, expected_rows: tuple[int, int]): findings = [] # 1. Schema and value constraints try: ServingSchema.validate(df, lazy=True) except pa.errors.SchemaErrors as e: for _, row in e.failure_cases.iterrows(): VIOLATIONS.labels(str(row["column"]), str(row["check"])).inc() findings.append(f"{row['column']}: {row['check']} failed " f"({row['failure_case']})") # 2. Volume — a batch at 40% of normal size is a broken extract lo, hi = expected_rows ROW_COUNT.labels("serving").set(len(df)) if not lo <= len(df) <= hi: findings.append(f"Row count {len(df):,} outside expected [{lo:,}, {hi:,}]") # 3. Null rates — alert on CHANGE, not an absolute threshold for col in df.columns: rate = df[col].isna().mean() NULL_RATE.labels(col).set(rate) baseline = BASELINE_NULL_RATES.get(col, 0) if rate > baseline + 0.05 and rate > 0.01: findings.append(f"{col}: null rate {rate:.1%} vs baseline {baseline:.1%}") # 4. New categorical values — an unseen category becomes an all-zeros encoding for col in CATEGORICAL_COLS: unseen = set(df[col].dropna().unique()) - KNOWN_CATEGORIES[col] if unseen: findings.append(f"{col}: unseen categories {sorted(unseen)[:5]}") # 5. Sentinel-value detection — THE Chennai check for col in NUMERIC_COLS: top = df[col].value_counts(normalize=True, dropna=True) if len(top) and top.iloc[0] > 0.10 and top.index[0] in (-1, -999, 0, 9999): findings.append(f"{col}: suspicious value {top.index[0]} in " f"{top.iloc[0]:.1%} of rows — possible sentinel") return findings ``` **That fifth check is the one worth copying.** A numeric column where 12% of values are exactly `-1` is almost never a genuine measurement. Adding it costs five lines and catches an entire class of upstream failure. **Alert on change rather than absolute thresholds.** A null rate going from 0.1% to 4% is a real event even though 4% sounds tolerable; a column that has always been 30% null is not. ##### Data drift versus concept drift The distinction that determines whether retraining will help. **Data drift (covariate shift):** `P(X)` changes, `P(y|X)` stays the same. Your applicant mix shifts toward Tier-3 cities. The relationship between features and default is unchanged; the model is now operating in a region where it has less training support. **Concept drift:** `P(y|X)` changes. A new UPI fraud technique means the same transaction pattern now indicates fraud when it previously did not. The learned relationship is simply wrong now. ``` Data drift: P(X) changes, P(y|X) same → model may still be fine Concept drift: P(y|X) changes → model is now wrong Label drift: P(y) changes → recalibration may suffice ``` Concrete examples, which is the assignment: **Data drift.** A grocery delivery model trained mostly on urban Bengaluru customers is deployed to Tier-2 towns after an expansion. Basket sizes, order frequency and payment modes all shift. But the *relationship* — that customers with declining order frequency churn — still holds. Detection: PSI on the input features spikes while the relationship metrics hold. **Concept drift.** A demand forecasting model trained pre-2020 encounters the pandemic. The same inputs (day of week, season, promotion flag) now map to completely different demand. Detection: input distributions may look normal, but performance collapses. Only labels or a proxy reveal it. Gama et al. classify drift by shape: | Shape | Pattern | Example | |---|---|---| | **Sudden** | Abrupt change | A policy change, a competitor launch | | **Gradual** | Slow transition | Changing customer preferences | | **Incremental** | Steady trend | Inflation, gradual portfolio shift | | **Recurring** | Cyclical return | Diwali season, month-end salary cycles | **Recurring drift generates the most false alarms** in Indian retail and fintech. A festival spike is not a regression, and a detector that alerts every Diwali gets muted — after which it catches nothing. ##### Detecting drift ```python import numpy as np from scipy.stats import ks_2samp, chi2_contingency, wasserstein_distance def psi(expected: np.ndarray, actual: np.ndarray, bins: int = 10) -> float: """Population Stability Index — the industry standard for tabular drift.""" edges = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)) edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf e = np.histogram(expected, edges)[0] / len(expected) a = np.histogram(actual, edges)[0] / len(actual) e, a = np.clip(e, 1e-6, None), np.clip(a, 1e-6, None) return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e))) def drift_report(reference: pd.DataFrame, current: pd.DataFrame, num_cols: list[str], cat_cols: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame: rows = [] for c in num_cols: ref, cur = reference[c].dropna(), current[c].dropna() rows.append({ "feature": c, "type": "numeric", "psi": psi(ref, cur), "wasserstein": wasserstein_distance(ref, cur) / (ref.std() + 1e-9), "ks_p": ks_2samp(ref, cur).pvalue, "mean_shift_sd": (cur.mean() - ref.mean()) / (ref.std() + 1e-9), }) for c in cat_cols: ref_dist = reference[c].value_counts(normalize=True) cur_dist = current[c].value_counts(normalize=True) all_cats = sorted(set(ref_dist.index) | set(cur_dist.index)) e = np.clip([ref_dist.get(k, 0) for k in all_cats], 1e-6, None) a = np.clip([cur_dist.get(k, 0) for k in all_cats], 1e-6, None) rows.append({ "feature": c, "type": "categorical", "psi": float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e))), "new_categories": sorted(set(cur_dist.index) - set(ref_dist.index))[:5], }) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) df["severity"] = pd.cut(df.psi, bins=[-np.inf, 0.10, 0.25, np.inf], labels=["stable", "moderate", "significant"]) return df.sort_values("psi", ascending=False) ``` **PSI thresholds** by convention: below 0.10 stable, 0.10 to 0.25 moderate and worth investigating, above 0.25 significant. **Prefer PSI to statistical tests on large samples.** With two million production rows, a KS test rejects the null for a shift of no practical consequence. PSI is an **effect-size** measure, not a p-value, which is exactly what you want when sample size is large and arbitrary. For high-dimensional or unstructured data, the **domain classifier** is the general-purpose detector: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier def domain_classifier_drift(reference: pd.DataFrame, current: pd.DataFrame) -> dict: """If a model can tell reference from current, the distributions differ.""" X = pd.concat([reference, current], ignore_index=True) y = np.r_[np.zeros(len(reference)), np.ones(len(current))] clf = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, random_state=42) auc = cross_val_score(clf, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean() clf.fit(X, y) from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance imp = permutation_importance(clf, X, y, n_repeats=5, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1) culprits = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=X.columns).nlargest(5) return {"drift_auc": auc, "verdict": "significant drift" if auc > 0.70 else "mild drift" if auc > 0.60 else "no meaningful drift", "top_drifting_features": culprits.round(4).to_dict()} ``` An AUC near 0.5 means the two samples are indistinguishable — no drift. Above 0.7 means substantial drift, and the feature importances tell you **which** features drifted, which is the actionable part. **Prediction drift** is the cheapest early warning available, because it needs no labels at all: ```python PRED_MEAN = Gauge("prediction_score_mean", "", ["model_version"]) PRED_P95 = Gauge("prediction_score_p95", "", ["model_version"]) FLAG_RATE = Gauge("prediction_flag_rate", "", ["model_version"]) def prediction_drift(scores: np.ndarray, reference_scores: np.ndarray, model_version: str, threshold: float) -> dict: PRED_MEAN.labels(model_version).set(scores.mean()) PRED_P95.labels(model_version).set(np.percentile(scores, 95)) FLAG_RATE.labels(model_version).set((scores >= threshold).mean()) return { "psi": psi(reference_scores, scores), "mean_shift": scores.mean() - reference_scores.mean(), "flag_rate": float((scores >= threshold).mean()), "flag_rate_reference": float((reference_scores >= threshold).mean()), } ``` If the mean predicted probability moves from 0.017 to 0.061 in a week, something changed — inputs, upstream code, or the world. In the Chennai case the score distribution would have shifted visibly within days. ##### Evidently Evidently packages most of this with good defaults and readable HTML reports. ```python from evidently import Report from evidently.presets import (DataDriftPreset, DataSummaryPreset, ClassificationPreset, TargetDriftPreset) report = Report(metrics=[ DataDriftPreset(), DataSummaryPreset(), ]) result = report.run(reference_data=reference_df, current_data=current_df) result.save_html("reports/drift_2026-03-15.html") # Extract for alerting rather than eyeballing payload = result.dict() n_drifted = payload["metrics"][0]["result"]["number_of_drifted_columns"] share = payload["metrics"][0]["result"]["share_of_drifted_columns"] print(f"{n_drifted} drifted columns ({share:.1%})") # With labels available, add performance perf = Report(metrics=[ClassificationPreset(probas_threshold=0.31), TargetDriftPreset()]) perf_result = perf.run(reference_data=ref_with_labels, current_data=cur_with_labels) ``` Evidently also supports **test suites** that produce pass/fail rather than a report to read: ```python from evidently import TestSuite from evidently.tests import (TestShareOfDriftedColumns, TestColumnDrift, TestNumberOfMissingValues, TestNumberOfRows) suite = TestSuite(tests=[ TestNumberOfRows(gte=40_000, lte=200_000), TestNumberOfMissingValues(lte=0.05), TestShareOfDriftedColumns(lt=0.30), TestColumnDrift(column_name="monthly_income_inr", stattest="psi", stattest_threshold=0.25), TestColumnDrift(column_name="months_since_enquiry", stattest="psi", stattest_threshold=0.25), ]) suite.run(reference_data=reference_df, current_data=current_df) if not suite.as_dict()["summary"]["all_passed"]: raise ValueError(f"Monitoring tests failed: {suite.as_dict()['summary']}") ``` **Test suites belong in the pipeline; reports belong in the review.** A test that fails a batch is actionable; an HTML report nobody opens is not. ##### Layer 4: performance with delayed labels The hard problem, and the common case. Loan defaults take 90 days; chargebacks 45 to 120; churn 30. Six techniques, layered: **1. Proxy labels.** Find a fast signal correlated with the true one, validate the correlation once, then monitor the proxy daily. ```python def validate_proxy(historical: pd.DataFrame, proxy: str, true_label: str) -> dict: """Confirm the proxy actually predicts the outcome before relying on it.""" from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score from scipy.stats import pointbiserialr mask = historical[true_label].notna() & historical[proxy].notna() return { "correlation": float(pointbiserialr(historical.loc[mask, proxy], historical.loc[mask, true_label])[0]), "auc": float(roc_auc_score(historical.loc[mask, true_label], historical.loc[mask, proxy])), "n": int(mask.sum()), } # First-EMI bounce at 30 days as a proxy for 90-day default print(validate_proxy(history, "emi_bounce_30d", "defaulted_90d")) ``` **2. Prediction distribution monitoring**, as above — no labels required. **3. Uncertainty tracking.** Rising predictive entropy or falling maximum probability across the population signals the model is encountering unfamiliar inputs. **4. Human review sampling.** Send 0.5–2% of predictions to expert review. Small sample, real ground truth, arriving in days. **5. Cohort-based backfill** with explicit label coverage: ```python def cohort_performance(maturity_days: int = 90) -> pd.DataFrame: """Only evaluate cohorts old enough to have labels — and say how mature.""" query = f""" SELECT date_trunc('week', p.predicted_at) AS cohort, p.model_version, count(*) AS n, avg(case when l.label is not null then 1 else 0 end) AS label_coverage, avg(p.score) AS mean_score, pr_auc(l.label, p.score) FILTER (WHERE l.label IS NOT NULL) AS pr_auc FROM predictions p LEFT JOIN outcomes l USING (prediction_id) WHERE p.predicted_at < current_date - interval '{maturity_days} days' GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1 DESC """ return run_sql(query) ``` **Always report `label_coverage` alongside the metric.** A PR-AUC computed on 12% of a cohort is a preview, not a measurement — and probably a biased one, since the cases that resolve fastest are rarely representative. **6. Business KPIs.** Approval rate, alert volume, downstream conversion. These move within days and are what the business cares about anyway. ##### Logging: the foundation You cannot monitor what you did not log. ```python import structlog, uuid, time, hashlib log = structlog.get_logger() def predict_and_log(request, model, meta) -> dict: pid = str(uuid.uuid4()) t0 = time.perf_counter() features = build_features(request) score = float(model.predict_proba(features)[0, 1]) decision = "review" if score >= meta["threshold"] else "pass" log.info("prediction", prediction_id=pid, entity_id=hashlib.sha256((SALT + request.customer_id).encode() ).hexdigest()[:16], # DPDP-safe model_name=meta["model_name"], model_version=meta["version"], # ESSENTIAL feature_spec_hash=meta["feature_hash"], features=features.iloc[0].to_dict() if SAMPLE_THIS_ROW else None, score=score, threshold=meta["threshold"], decision=decision, latency_ms=(time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, ts=pd.Timestamp.now(tz="Asia/Kolkata").isoformat()) return {"prediction_id": pid, "score": score, "decision": decision} ``` Four non-negotiables. A **`prediction_id`** the outcome table can join on. The **`model_version`**, so a regression is attributable to a deployment. **Hashed identifiers** rather than raw ones — raw phone numbers or Aadhaar in log storage is a DPDP exposure. And **sampled feature logging** in high-volume systems: 5% of 40 million daily predictions is ample for drift statistics at a fraction of the storage cost. ##### Alerting that people trust ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Metrics collected] --> B{Severity} B -->|P1: service down, score collapse| C[Page on-call immediately] B -->|P2: PSI > 0.25 sustained, perf below floor| D[Ticket + Slack, next business day] B -->|P3: PSI 0.10-0.25, minor anomaly| E[Weekly digest] C --> F[Runbook: rollback, disable, escalate] D --> G[Diagnose: data quality? drift? concept?] G --> H{Upstream data broken?} H -->|Yes| I[FIX THE PIPELINE — do not retrain] H -->|No| J{Concept drift confirmed?} J -->|Yes| K[Trigger retraining candidate] J -->|No| L[Document and monitor] ``` ```python ALERT_RULES = { "score_mean_shift": {"threshold": 0.05, "windows": 2, "severity": "P1"}, "psi_any_feature": {"threshold": 0.25, "windows": 3, "severity": "P2"}, "share_drifted": {"threshold": 0.30, "windows": 2, "severity": "P2"}, "null_rate_increase": {"threshold": 0.05, "windows": 1, "severity": "P2"}, "unseen_categories": {"threshold": 1, "windows": 1, "severity": "P2"}, "pr_auc_below_floor": {"threshold": 0.30, "windows": 1, "severity": "P1"}, } def evaluate_alerts(history: pd.DataFrame, rules: dict) -> list[dict]: """Fire only on SUSTAINED conditions — single-window alerts create fatigue.""" fired = [] for metric, rule in rules.items(): recent = history[metric].tail(rule["windows"]) if len(recent) == rule["windows"] and (recent > rule["threshold"]).all(): fired.append({"metric": metric, "severity": rule["severity"], "values": recent.tolist(), "runbook": RUNBOOKS[metric]}) return fired ``` Four rules that keep alerts trusted. **Require sustained conditions** — PSI above 0.25 for three consecutive windows, not one. **Suppress known seasonality** with explicit windows around Diwali, month-end and quarter-end. **Route by severity** rather than paging everyone. And **attach a runbook link** to every alert; one nobody can act on gets muted, and a muted channel is how the next Chennai incident happens. ```python SEASONAL_SUPPRESSION = [ ("2026-10-15", "2026-11-15", "Diwali season"), ("2026-03-25", "2026-04-05", "Financial year end"), ] def is_suppressed(date: pd.Timestamp) -> str | None: for start, end, reason in SEASONAL_SUPPRESSION: if pd.Timestamp(start) <= date <= pd.Timestamp(end): return reason return None ``` ##### Retraining triggers Retraining is a **response to a diagnosis**, not a reflex. | Signal | Correct response | |---|---| | Data quality failure | **Fix the pipeline.** Retraining bakes in the corruption. | | Data drift alone | Investigate. The model may still generalise. | | Concept drift confirmed | Retrain. | | Performance below floor | Retrain, and consider rolling back while it trains. | | Scheduled interval elapsed | Retrain as a floor, not a primary trigger. | ```python def should_retrain() -> tuple[bool, list[str]]: reasons = [] # HARD GATE: never retrain on data that failed quality checks if not latest_quality_check_passed(): return False, ["data quality gate failed — fix upstream first"] if get_drift_metric("share_drifted", windows=3) > 0.30: reasons.append("sustained input drift across >30% of features") if get_performance("pr_auc_proxy") < PERFORMANCE_FLOOR: reasons.append("proxy performance below floor") if count_new_labels() > 20_000: reasons.append("sufficient new labelled data") if days_since_training() > 45: reasons.append("scheduled floor reached") return bool(reasons), reasons ``` **The data-quality gate blocking retraining is the most important line there.** In Chennai, automated retraining would have learned the `-1` corruption as a real signal and made the problem permanent. And **retraining must never auto-deploy.** It produces a challenger that goes through the same evaluation gates and human approval as any other candidate. ##### A monitoring runbook The artifact that turns an alert into a resolution. ```markdown ## Runbook: churn-scorer monitoring ### Alert: score_mean_shift (P1) Mean predicted probability moved >0.05 in 2 consecutive windows. 1. Check the data-quality dashboard first. A pipeline break is far more likely than a genuine shift of this size. 2. Compare the current feature distributions against reference (Evidently report, auto-generated hourly at /reports/drift_latest.html). 3. If one feature dominates the drift, check with the upstream owner — schema changes and unit changes are the usual causes. 4. If no upstream cause is found, roll back to the previous champion and investigate with the pressure off. **Rollback:** `python -m ops.rollback --model churn-scorer` **Measured time to recovery:** 4 minutes. ### Alert: psi_any_feature > 0.25 (P2) 1. Identify which features drifted (domain classifier importances). 2. Determine whether this is expected seasonality — check the suppression calendar before escalating. 3. If genuine and sustained, open a retraining ticket. Do NOT retrain automatically. ### Known seasonal patterns - Diwali (Oct–Nov): order volume +180%, basket size +40%. Expected. - Month-end (last 5 days): transaction velocity +25%. Expected. ### Escalation P1: page the on-call data scientist. P2: ticket to the ML team backlog. ``` ##### Common mistakes - Monitoring service health and calling it model monitoring. - No schema validation at serving, so a sentinel like `-1` passes silently. - KS tests on millions of rows, alerting on statistically significant but meaningless shifts. - Alerting on a single window instead of a sustained condition. - No seasonality suppression, so every festival triggers a false alarm. - Not logging `model_version` with predictions, making attribution impossible. - Reporting cohort metrics without label coverage. - Waiting for true labels when a validated proxy was available in 30 days. - Auto-retraining on drift without a data-quality gate. - Raw PII in prediction logs. ##### Hands-on Take a model's reference dataset and construct a shifted "production" dataset — inject a sentinel value into one feature, shift another's mean, and add an unseen category. Use Evidently to generate a drift report and confirm it identifies all three. Then implement the domain-classifier check and verify its feature importances point at the same columns. Finally, define an alert rule with a sustained-window condition and demonstrate that a single-window blip does not fire it while a genuine three-window shift does. For the mini-project, build a monitoring setup that computes drift and performance metrics on incoming batches, produces Evidently dashboards, and defines alerting and retraining-trigger logic. Include all four layers: service metrics, data-quality checks with sentinel detection, drift monitoring with PSI and prediction-distribution tracking, and cohort-based performance with label coverage reported. Add a proxy-label pipeline with a validated correlation to the true outcome, seasonal suppression for Indian festival periods, and a written runbook covering what to do for each alert type with a measured rollback time. Simulate the Chennai incident end to end and confirm your system catches it within one window. For the assignment, explain the difference between data drift and concept drift with a concrete example of each and how you would detect them. Be specific about which detection layer catches which, and about the case where input distributions look completely normal while performance collapses — because that is the one that requires labels or a proxy and cannot be caught any other way. ##### Key takeaways - Green service dashboards say nothing about correctness; models fail by producing plausible wrong answers. - Data-quality validation at serving catches more real incidents than any drift statistic, and catches them fastest. - Data drift changes `P(X)` and may be survivable; concept drift changes `P(y|X)` and means the model is wrong. - Use PSI (effect size) over p-values on large samples, and a domain classifier to find which features drifted. - Diagnose before retraining — a pipeline break must be fixed upstream, and retraining must never auto-deploy.
practical_task_reference: Take a deployed model's reference dataset and a shifted 'production' dataset, use Evidently to generate a data-drift report, and set a rule that would trigger an alert or retraining.
